title.en: Sixteen Years Behind the Golden Doors: Tupac Inca Presented to the Sun
title.zh: 金門後十六年:圖帕克·印加獻於太陽之前

region.en: House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 42, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: He then said that he named his son Tupac Inca, and ordered him to come forth from the house. He had been there for 15 or 16 years to be brought up, without any one seeing him except very rarely and as a great favour. He was now shown to the people, and the Inca presently ordered a fringe of gold to be placed in the hand of the image of the Sun. After Tupac Inca had made his obeisance to his father, they went before the image of the Sun, made their sacrifices and offered capa cocha to that deity; then they offered the new Inca Tupac Yupanqui, beseeching the Sun to protect and foster him, and to make him so that all should hold and judge him to be a child of the Sun and father of his people. The priests took the fringe from the hands of the image, which they call mascapaycha, and placed it over the head of Tupac Inca Yupanqui until it rested on his forehead. He was declared Inca Ccapac and seated in front of the Sun on a seat of gold, garnished with emeralds. Seated there, they clothed him in the ccapac uncu, placed the suntur paucar in his hand, and the priests raised him on their shoulders. His brother Amaru Tupac Inca, the eldest legitimate son who had been named successor years before, came to see him: when Amaru saw him in such majesty of wealth and surroundings he fell on his face to the earth, adoring, offering sacrifices and obedience; on learning that it was his brother, Tupac Inca raised him and saluted him in the face.
summary.zh: 印加王宣布立子圖帕克·印加為儲,命他出屋。此子在屋中養育十五六年,除極少數特許之外,無人得見。此時他方被引見於民;印加王命人將金王纓置於太陽神像手中。圖帕克·印加向父王行禮後,眾人先向太陽神像獻祭,並行卡帕-科查人祭;再獻上新印加圖帕克·尤潘琪,祈求太陽護佑他,使萬民奉他為太陽之子、民眾之父。祭司從神像手中取下王纓——即「瑪斯卡帕恰」——戴於圖帕克·印加·尤潘琪頭上,直至額前。他被宣布為「卡帕克·印加」,坐於太陽像前鑲祖母綠的金座之上;眾人為他披上卡帕克上衣,把孫圖爾-保卡爾放入他手中,祭司們將他扛上肩頭。此前曾被立為儲的嫡長子阿瑪魯·圖帕克·印加前來相見;阿瑪魯見兄弟富貴威儀如此,當即伏地叩拜,獻祭稱臣;得知確是自己的兄弟,圖帕克·印加扶他起來,與他貼面相慶。

sensitivity.note: The secluded heir revealed; the mascapaycha taken from the image's own hands as in Pachacuti's coronation.

passages.text: He then said that he named his son Tupac Inca, and ordered him to come forth from the house. He had been there for 15 or 16 years to be brought up, without any one seeing him except very rarely and as a great favour. He was now shown to the people, and the Inca presently ordered a fringe of gold to be placed in the hand of the image of the Sun... Then they offered the new Inca Tupac Yupanqui, beseeching the Sun to protect and foster him, and to make him so that all should hold and judge him to be a child of the Sun and father of his people.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 42 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The priests took the fringe from the hands of the image, which they call mascapaycha, and placed it over the head of Tupac Inca Yupanqui until it rested on his forehead. He was declared Inca Ccapac and seated in front of the Sun on a seat of gold, called duho, garnished with emeralds and other precious stones. Seated there, they clothed him in the ccapac uncu, placed the suntur paucar in his hand, gave him the other insignia of Inca, and the priests raised him on their shoulders.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 42 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: There came to the Inca Pachacuti his son Amaru Tupac Inca, who had been named by his father as his successor some years before... he desired to see him and offer sacrifice to him. When Amaru saw him in such majesty of wealth and surroundings, he fell on his face to the earth, adoring, offering sacrifices and obedience. On learning that it was his brother, Tupac Inca raised him and saluted him in the face.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 43 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Eyebrows Blown in Offering: The Roads Cleared for Tupac Inca
title.zh: 吹毛為獻:為圖帕克·印加清道的眾生

region.zh: 欽查蘇尤大道(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 44, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Tupac went in such pomp and majesty that, where he passed, no one dared to look him in the face, in such veneration was he held. The people left the roads along which he had to pass and, ascending the hills on either side, worshipped and adored. They pulled out their eyebrows and eyelashes, and blowing on them, they made offering to the Inca. Others offered handfuls of a very precious herb called coca. When he arrived at the villages, he put on the dress and head-gear of that district, for all were different in their dress and head-gear: for Inca Yupanqui, so as to know each nation he had conquered, ordered that each one should have a special dress and head-gear, which they call pillu, llaytu and chuco, different one from the other, so as to be easily distinguished and recognized. Seating himself, Tupac Inca made a solemn sacrifice of animals and birds, burning them in a fire kindled in his presence; and in this way they worshipped the sun, which they believed to be God.
summary.zh: 圖帕克出行,儀仗威嚴:所過之處,無人敢直視其面。百姓離開王駕必經的道路,登上兩側山坡,頂禮膜拜;他們拔下自己的眉毛睫毛,向王吹獻為禮;另有人捧上名貴的古柯葉為獻。王至各村,便換上該地的服飾頭冠——各族衣冠各異;印加·尤潘琪為便於辨識所征各族,特命各族服飾頭飾各有專式,名為「皮尤」「勞圖」「丘科」,一望可辨。圖帕克·印加端坐,就地焚燒牲畜飛鳥,行莊嚴獻祭——他們如此崇拜太陽,奉之為神。

sensitivity.note: The eyebrow-blowing offering recorded as the standard act of reverence before the king.

passages.text: Tupac went in such pomp and majesty that, where he passed, no one dared to look him in the face, in such veneration was he held. The people left the roads along which he had to pass and, ascending the hills on either side, worshipped and adored. They pulled out their eyebrows and eyelashes, and blowing on them, they made offering to the Inca. Others offered handfuls of a very precious herb called coca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 44 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he arrived at the villages, he put on the dress and head-gear of that district, for all were different in their dress and head-gear as they are now. For Inca Yupanqui, so as to know each nation he had conquered, ordered that each one should have a special dress and head-gear, which they call pillu, llaytu and chuco, different one from the other, so as to be easily distinguished and recognized.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 44 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Antarqui Flies Over the Sea: The Necromancer Who Reconnoitred the Islands
title.zh: 安塔爾基飛越重洋:偵島的巫師

region.en: Islands of Avachumbi and Ninachumbi, western sea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西海阿瓦瓊比與尼納瓊比群島(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 46, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: There arrived at Tumbez some merchants who had come by sea from the west, navigating in balsas with sails. They gave information of the land whence they came, which consisted of some islands called Avachumbi and Ninachumbi, where there were many people and much gold. Tupac Inca was a man of lofty and ambitious ideas, and was not satisfied with the regions he had already conquered. So he determined to challenge a happy fortune, and see if it would favour him by sea. Yet he did not lightly believe the navigating merchants, for such men, being great talkers, ought not to be credited too readily. In order to obtain fuller information, he called a man who accompanied him in his conquests, named Antarqui, who, they all declare, was a great necromancer and could even fly through the air. Tupac Inca asked him whether what the merchant mariners said was true. Antarqui answered, after having thought the matter well out, that what they said was true, and that he would go there first. They say that he accomplished this by his arts, traversed the route, saw the islands, their people and riches, and, returning, gave certain information of all to Tupac Inca.
summary.zh: 通貝斯港來了幾名自西方乘帆筏渡海而來的商人。他們說起故鄉所在:海中有島,名「阿瓦瓊比」與「尼納瓊比」,人煙稠密,黃金遍地。圖帕克·印加志存高遠,不滿足於已得之地,決意試探海上的命運。然而他並不輕信這些誇誇其談的水商;為求確證,他召來隨征的安塔爾基——眾人都說此人法力高強,甚至能凌空飛行。圖帕克問他:商人所言可真?安塔爾基深思之後答道:所言屬實,而且他願先行探路。相傳他果然以法術飛越航線,親見群島、島民與富饒,然後回報,把一切確切告知圖帕克·印加。

sensitivity.note: The flying necromancer as pre-expedition scout; Markham's note identifies the islands (perhaps) with the Galapagos.

title.en: The Jawbone of a Horse: Tupac Inca's Voyage to Avachumbi
title.zh: 馬的頜骨:圖帕克·印加的遠航

region.en: Islands of Avachumbi and Ninachumbi (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿瓦瓊比與尼納瓊比群島(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 46, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The Inca, having this certainty, determined to go there. He caused an immense number of balsas to be constructed, in which he embarked more than 20,000 chosen men, taking with him as captains Huaman Achachi, Cunti Yupanqui, Quihual Tupac (all Hanan-cuzcos), Yancan Mayta, Quisu Mayta, Cachimapaca Macus Yupanqui, Llimpita Usca Mayta (Hurin-cuzcos); his brother Tilca Yupanqui being general of the whole fleet. Tupac Inca navigated and sailed on until he discovered the islands of Avachumbi and Ninachumbi, and returned, bringing back with him black people, gold, a chair of brass, and a skin and jaw bone of a horse. These trophies were preserved in the fortress of Cuzco until the Spaniards came. An Inca now living had charge of this skin and jaw bone of a horse. He gave this account, and the rest who were present corroborated it. His name is Urco Huaranca. The duration of this expedition was nine months, others say a year, and, as he was so long absent, every one believed he was dead. But to deceive them and make them think that news of Tupac Inca had come, Apu Yupanqui, his general of the land army, made rejoicings. This was afterwards commented upon to his disadvantage, and it was said that he rejoiced because he was pleased that Tupac Inca Yupanqui did not appear. It cost him his life.
summary.zh: 印加王既有確證,便決意遠征。他命人造筏無數,載精兵兩萬餘人;將領有瓜曼·阿查奇、昆蒂·尤潘琪、基瓦爾·圖帕克(皆哈南庫斯科),揚坎·馬雅塔、基蘇·馬雅塔、卡奇馬帕卡·馬庫斯·尤潘琪、伊利皮塔·烏斯卡·馬雅塔(皆烏林庫斯科);其弟蒂爾卡·尤潘琪統領全船隊;陸軍則由阿普·尤潘琪統率留守。圖帕克·印加揚帆遠航,直至發現阿瓦瓊比與尼納瓊比二島,然後返航——帶回黑人、黃金、一把銅椅,還有一張馬皮與一副馬的頜骨。這些戰利品一直珍藏在庫斯科的堡壘中,直至西班牙人到來。尚在人世的一位印加老人烏爾科·瓦蘭卡,曾親自保管那張馬皮與馬頜骨,如此作證,在場眾人皆附和其說。遠征歷時九月,或說一年;因王久出不歸,舉國都當他已死。陸軍統帥阿普·尤潘琪為安人心,詐稱圖帕克·印加有信,下令歡慶——此事後來成為他的罪狀:人們說他歡慶,是因為高興王不回來。這條謠言,竟要了他的性命。

sensitivity.note: The most extraordinary trans-Pacific claim in Andean tradition; the horse relics are the evidentiary core (Sarmiento swore witnesses) and remain a famous crux.

Apu Yupanqui was left in command of the army which remained on land.

title.en: I Was Born as a Flower of the Field: Pachacuti's Dying Words
title.zh: 我生如野花:帕查庫提的臨終之歌

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 47, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Being in the highest prosperity and sovereignty of his life, he fell ill of a grave infirmity, and, feeling that he was at the point of death, he sent for all his sons who were then in the city. In their presence he first divided all his jewels and contents of his wardrobe. Next he made them plough furrows in token that they were vassals of their brother, and that they had to eat by the sweat of their hands. He also gave them arms in token that they were to fight for their brother. He next sent for the Incas orejones of Cuzco, his relations, and for Tupac Inca his son, to whom he spoke with a few words: 'Son! you now see how many great nations I leave to you, and you know what labour they have cost me. Mind that you are the man to keep and augment them. No one must raise his two eyes against you and live, even if he be your own brother. I leave you these our relations that they may be your councillors. Care for them and they shall serve you. When I am dead, take care of my body, and put it in my houses at Patallacta. Have my golden image in the House of the Sun, and make my subjects, in all the provinces, offer up solemn sacrifice, after which keep the feast of purucaya, that I may go to rest with my father the Sun.' Having finished his speech they say that he began to sing in a low and sad voice, with words of his own language: 'I was born as a flower of the field, as a flower I was cherished in my youth, I came to my full age, I grew old, now I am withered and die.' Having uttered these words, he laid his head upon a pillow and expired.
summary.zh: 正當盛年威福之極,帕查庫提忽染重疾,自知大限將至,便召在城諸子。當著他們的面,他先分完所有珍寶衣物;再命諸子扶犁開溝——以示他們是兄弟的藩屬,當以雙手汗水謀食;又授兵刃——以示他們當為兄弟而戰。隨後召庫斯科的印加耳垂貴胄與其子圖帕克·印加,簡言囑道:「兒啊!你看我留給你多少大邦,你知我為此耗費多少辛勞。你要守成,更要拓土。任何人不得仰視你而活——縱是你的親兄弟也不行。我把這些親族交給你作謀臣;善待他們,他們便侍奉你。我死之後,妥善安置我的遺體,放入帕塔利亞克的我的宮室;把我的金像供在太陽之屋;命各行省臣民舉行隆重獻祭,然後行普魯卡亞之祭——好讓我與我父太陽同歸安息。」言畢,相傳他以本族語言低聲悲唱:「我生如野地之花,幼時如花受呵護,及至成年又衰老,如今枯萎而凋零。」唱罷,他頭枕憑几,溘然長逝。

sensitivity.note: The flower death-song (Castilian rendering of a Quechua elegy) and the furrow-ploughing vassalage rite at the deathbed.

title.en: Condin Savana the Shapechanger: Hunting Smoke in the Forests of the Antis
title.zh: 變形者孔丁-薩瓦納:安蒂林海中獵煙

region.en: Forests of Antisuyu, east of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科以東安蒂蘇尤林海(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 49, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The forests were very dense and full of evil places; so that they could not force their way through, nor did they know what direction to take in order to reach the settlements of the natives, which were well concealed in the thick vegetation. To find them the explorers climbed up the highest trees, and pointed out the places where they could see smoke rising. So they worked away at road making through the undergrowth until they lost that sign of inhabitants and found another. In this way the Inca made a road where it seemed impossible to make one. The Sinchi of the greater part of these provinces of the Antis was Condin Savana, of whom they say that he was a great wizard and enchanter, and they had the belief, and even now they affirm that he could turn himself into different shapes. Tupac Inca and his captains penetrated into this region of the Antis, which consists of the most terrible and fearful forests, with many rivers, where they endured immense toil, and the people who came from Peru suffered from the change of climate; the soldiers became sick, and many died. Tupac Inca himself, with a third of his men who came with him to conquer, were lost in the forests, and wandered for a long time, without knowing whether to go in one direction or another, until he fell in with Uturuncu Achachi who put him on the route.
summary.zh: 安蒂的森林密不透風,兇險四伏;大軍無法強行穿過,又不知土人村落藏於何處——全都隱沒在濃密的草木之中。探路人只好攀上最高的樹,瞭望何處炊煙升起,便朝那裡砍路開道;待到煙跡消失,再尋新煙,如此節節推進。印加王就這樣在看似無路之地開出了一條路。這些安蒂省份大部歸辛奇孔丁-薩瓦納統轄;相傳他是位大巫師、大幻術家,能隨意變換形體——至今人們猶如此深信。圖帕克·印加與諸將深入這片最可怖的林海,河川縱橫,勞苦不堪;來自乾寒秘魯的兵士水土不服,病者甚眾,死者相繼。圖帕克·印加本人連同三分之一的部眾迷失林中,長久徘徊,不知何往,直至遇上烏圖倫庫·阿查奇,方才認路歸隊。

sensitivity.note: Amazonian frontier campaign; the shapeshifting sinchi as guardian of the forest world.

passages.text: The forests were very dense and full of evil places; so that they could not force their way through, nor did they know what direction to take in order to reach the settlements of the natives, which were well concealed in the thick vegetation. To find them the explorers climbed up the highest trees, and pointed out the places where they could see smoke rising... In this way the Inca made a road where it seemed impossible to make one.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 49 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sinchi of the greater part of these provinces of the Antis was Condin Savana, of whom they say that he was a great wizard and enchanter, and they had the belief, and even now they affirm that he could turn himself into different shapes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 49 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tupac Inca himself, with a third of his men who came with him to conquer, were lost in the forests, and wandered for a long time, without knowing whether to go in one direction or another until he fell in with Uturuncu Achachi who put him on the route.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 49 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The False Pachacuti: Coaquiri Steals a Dead Man's Name
title.zh: 偽帕查庫提:科阿基里盜用亡王之名

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 49, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: During the campaign an Indian of the Collas, named Coaquiri, fled from his company, reached the Collao, and spread the report that Tupac Inca was dead. He said that there was no longer an Inca, that they should all rise, and that he would be their leader. Presently he took the name of Pachacuti, the Collas rose, and chose him as their captain. This news reached Tupac Inca in Anti-suyu where he was in the career of conquest. He resolved to march against the Collas and punish them. He left the forests, leaving Uturuncu Achachi to complete the conquest, with orders to return into Peru when that service was completed, but not to enter Cuzco triumphing until the Inca should come. Having returned from the Antis, he increased his army and advanced to the Collao. The Collas had constructed four strong places at Llallaua, Asillo, Arapa, and Pucara. The Inca captured the chiefs and the leader of all, who was Chuca-chucay Pachacuti Coaquiri - afterwards these were the drummers of Inca Tupac.
summary.zh: 征戰期間,一名科利亞人科阿基里脫隊而逃,回到科利亞奧,散佈流言說圖帕克·印加已死。他說:印加已無,眾人當起事,他來做首領。不久他便自取「帕查庫提」之名;科利亞人群起,推他為帥。消息傳到正在安蒂蘇尤征戰的圖帕克·印加耳中,他決意回師討伐。他離開林海,留烏圖倫庫·阿查奇完成征服,命其事畢返回秘魯,但非待印加王親至,不得擅自凱旋入庫斯科。圖帕克·印加自安蒂回師,擴軍進逼科利亞奧。科利亞人築四座要塞於利亞勞阿、阿西略、阿拉帕、普卡拉。印加王擒獲諸酋,連同他們的總頭領「丘卡-丘卡伊·帕查庫提」科阿基里——這批人後來都成了圖帕克·印加的鼓手。

sensitivity.note: Name-theft as rebellion; the captured pretender turned royal drummer is a pointed humiliation.

He said that there was no longer an Inca, that they should all rise and that he would be their leader. Presently he took the name of Pachacuti, the Collas rose, and chose him as their captain.

passages.text: The Inca captured the chiefs and the leader of all, who was Chuca-chucay Pachacuti Coaquiri, he who, as we have said, fled from Anti-suyu. Afterwards these were the drummers of Inca Tupac. Finally, owing to the great diligence of Inca Tupac, although the war occupied some years, the Incas conquered and subdued all.
